IO::Select - OO interface to the "select" system call

SYNOPSIS
use IO::Select; my $sel = IO::Select->new(); $sel->add( \*STDIN ); $sel->add( $socket ); my $count = $sel->can_read( 10 ); # Wait 10 seconds for readability my @ready = $sel->can_read(); # Wait indefinitely for my $handle ( @ready ) { # Read from $handle }
DESCRIPTION
This module provides an object-oriented interface to the system’s select() call. It allows you to monitor multiple file descriptors for I/O readiness without blocking indefinitely on any single one.

IO::Socket - Object interface to socket communications

SYNOPSIS
use IO::Socket; $sock = IO::Socket::INET->new( Proto => "tcp", Listen => 5 ) or die "Cannot create socket: $@"; $client = $sock->accept; print $client "Hello, client\n"; close $sock;
DESCRIPTION
This module provides an object-oriented interface to socket communications. It is a subclass of IO.
CONSTRUCTOR ARGUMENTS
Blocking
If set to a false value, the socket will be created in non-blocking mode. Defaults to true.
Domain
The domain of the socket (e.g., AF_INET, AF_UNIX). Defaults to AF_INET.
Listen
The number of connections to queue for listening sockets. Defaults to SOMAXCONN.
Timeout
The timeout value for socket operations. Defaults to undef (no timeout). See also alarm.
Type
The type of the socket (e.g., SOCK_STREAM, SOCK_DGRAM). Defaults to SOCK_STREAM.
CONSTRUCTORS
new
METHODS
accept
Accepts a connection on a listening socket.
atmark
Returns true if the OOB mark is at the end of the urgent data.
autoflush
Whether to automatically flush the buffer after each write.
bind
Binds the socket to an address and port.
connected
Returns true if the socket is connected.
getsockopt
Gets socket options.
'- IO::Socket::'- 'SYNOPSIS': | use IO::Socket; my $sock = IO::Socket::INET->new( Proto => "tcp" ) or die "Could not create socket: $!"; my $client_sock = $sock->accept() or die "accept failed: $!"; print $client_sock "Hello, World!\n" or die "print failed: $!"; close($client_sock); close($sock); 'DESCRIPTION': | The IO::Socket module is a collection of classes that provide an object-oriented interface to the socket interfaces of various operating systems. The primary purpose of this module is to provide a common interface to the socket-related functionality that is available on most modern operating systems. This module provides classes that support the AF_INET domain sockets (also known as Internet domain sockets), the AF_UNIX domain sockets (also known as Unix domain sockets), and the AF_IMDS domain sockets (also known as Instra Messaging Domain sockets). 'MODULES': | IO::Socket::INET IO::Socket::UNIX IO::Socket::IP 'METHODS': | new open sockpair socket listen accept connect gethostbyname gethostbyaddr getservbyname getservbyport getsockopt setsockopt sockname peername shutdown protocol sockdomain socktype sockopt timeout recv send socketpair 'EXAMPLES': | See the synopsis above. 'LIMITATIONS': | None known. 'SEE ALSO': | IO::Socket::INET, IO::Socket::UNIX, IO::Socket::IP 'AUTHOR': | Tim Jenness (t.jenness@jach.hawaii.edu) 'COPYRIGHT': | Copyright (C) 1996-2001 Tim Jenness. All rights reserved. This program is free software; you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the same terms as Perl itself. '- IO::Socket::INET - Object interface for AF_INET domain sockets'- 'SYNOPSIS': | use IO::Socket; my $sock = IO::Socket::INET->new( PeerAddr => "www.perl.com:80", Proto => "tcp", ) or die "Could not connect to www.perl.com: $!"; print $sock "GET / HTTP/1.0\n\n"; my $response = do { local $/; <$sock> }; close($sock); my $server = IO::Socket::INET->new( LocalPort => 8080, Listen => 5, Proto => "tcp", ) or die "Could not create server socket: $!"; my $client = $server->accept(); if ($client) { print $client "Hello, client!\n"; close($client); } close($server); 'DESCRIPTION': | IO::Socket::INET is a class that provides an object-oriented interface to the AF_INET domain sockets (also known as Internet domain sockets). It is a subclass of IO::Socket. 'CONSTRUCTOR': | new ( [ARGS] ) The new method constructs a new IO::Socket::INET object. The following arguments are supported: PeerAddr => STRING PeerPort => STRING PeerHost => STRING LocalAddr => STRING LocalPort => STRING LocalHost => STRING Proto => STRING Listen => INTEGER ReuseAddr => BOOLEAN ReusePort => BOOLEAN Broadcast => BOOLEAN Sockopts => ARRAY V6Only => BOOLEAN MultiHomed => BOOLEAN Blocking => BOOLEAN Timeout => NUM 'METHODS': | sockaddr (), sockport (), sockhost (), peeraddr (), peerport (), peerhost () 'SEE ALSO': | IO::Socket, IO::Socket::IP, IO::Socket::UNIX 'AUTHOR': | Tim Jenness (t.jenness@jach.hawaii.edu) 'COPYRIGHT': | Copyright (C) 1996-2001 Tim Jenness. All rights reserved. This program is free software; you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the same terms as Perl itself. '- IO::Socket::IP, "IO::Socket::IP" - Family-neutral IP socket supporting both IPv4 and IPv6'- 'SYNOPSIS': | use IO::Socket::IP; # Connect to a peer my $sock = IO::Socket::IP->new( PeerHost => "www.perl.com", PeerPort => 80, Proto => "tcp", ) or die "Could not connect: $!"; print $sock "GET /\n"; my $response = do { local $/; <$sock> }; close($sock); # Create a server my $server = IO::Socket::IP->new( LocalPort => 8080, Listen => 5, Proto => "tcp", ) or die "Could not create server: $!"; my $client = $server->accept(); if ($client) { print $client "Hello, client!\n"; close($client); } close($server); 'DESCRIPTION': | IO::Socket::IP is a class that provides a family-neutral object-oriented interface to IP sockets. It supports both IPv4 and IPv6. It is a subclass of IO::Socket and provides a more convenient interface than IO::Socket::INET. 'REPLACING "IO::Socket" DEFAULT BEHAVIOUR': | By default, IO::Socket::INET prefers IPv6. If you want it to prefer IPv4, you can set the environment variable PERL_IPV4_PREFER=1. 'CONSTRUCTORS': | new ( ARGS ) new ( ONE_ARG ) 'new': | PeerHost => STRING, PeerService => STRING, PeerAddr => STRING, PeerPort => STRING, PeerAddrInfo => ARRAY, LocalHost => STRING, LocalService => STRING, LocalAddr => STRING, LocalPort => STRING, LocalAddrInfo => ARRAY, Family => INT, Type => INT, Proto => STRING or INT, GetAddrInfoFlags => INT, Listen => INT, ReuseAddr => BOOL, ReusePort => BOOL, Broadcast => BOOL, Sockopts => ARRAY, V6Only => BOOL, MultiHomed, Blocking => BOOL, Timeout => NUM When only one argument is provided, it is assumed to be a hash reference containing the same keys as the arguments described above. 'METHODS': | sockhost_service, sockhost, sockport, sockhostname, sockservice, sockaddr, peerhost_service, peerhost, peerport, peerhostname, peerservice, peeraddr, as_inet 'NON-BLOCKING': | The new method accepts a 'Blocking => BOOL' argument. If set to false, the socket will be created in non-blocking mode. '"PeerHost" AND "LocalHost" PARSING': | The PeerHost and LocalHost arguments can be a hostname or an IP address. If a hostname is provided, it will be resolved using the system's name resolution mechanism. If an IP address is provided, it will be used directly. The PeerService and LocalService arguments can be a service name (e.g., "http", "ftp") or a port number. If a service name is provided, it will be translated to a port number using the system's service database. 'split_addr': | This method splits a socket address into host and port components. 'join_addr': | This method joins a host and port into a socket address. '"IO::Socket::INET" INCOMPATIBILITIES': | IO::Socket::IP is not fully compatible with IO::Socket::INET. Specifically, the following methods are not supported: sockdomain, socktype, sockopt, timeout, recv, send, socketpair 'TODO': | - Add support for more socket options. - Add support for more protocol families. 'AUTHOR': | David O'Neill (dave@oneill.name) '- IO::Socket::UNIX - Object interface for AF_UNIX domain sockets'- 'SYNOPSIS': | use IO::Socket::UNIX; # Create a server my $server = IO::Socket::UNIX->new( LocalPath => "/tmp/my_socket", Listen => 5, ) or die "Could not create server socket: $!"; my $client = $server->accept(); if ($client) { print $client "Hello, client!\n"; close($client); } close($server); # Connect to a server my $sock = IO::Socket::UNIX->new( PeerPath => "/tmp/my_socket", ) or die "Could not connect to server: $!"; my $response = do { local $/; <$sock> }; close($sock); 'DESCRIPTION': | IO::Socket::UNIX is a class that provides an object-oriented interface to the AF_UNIX domain sockets (also known as Unix domain sockets). It is a subclass of IO::Socket. 'CONSTRUCTOR': | new ( [ARGS] ) The new method constructs a new IO::Socket::UNIX object. The following arguments are supported: LocalPath => STRING PeerPath => STRING Listen => INTEGER ReuseAddr => BOOLEAN ReusePort => BOOLEAN 'METHODS': | hostpath(), peerpath() 'SEE ALSO': | IO::Socket, IO::Socket::INET, IO::Socket::IP 'AUTHOR': | Tim Jenness (t.jenness@jach.hawaii.edu) 'COPYRIGHT': | Copyright (C) 1996-2001 Tim Jenness. All rights reserved. This program is free software; you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the same terms as Perl itself. '- IO::Uncompress::AnyInflate - Uncompress zlib-based (zip, gzip) file/buffer'- 'SYNOPSIS': | use IO::Uncompress::AnyInflate qw(anyinflate); # Decompress a gzip file to a scalar my $uncompressed = anyinflate("file.gz") or die "Decompression failed: $!"; # Decompress a zip file to a file anyinflate("archive.zip" => "output.tar") or die "Decompression failed: $!"; # Decompress a gzip stream to a filehandle open my $in, "<:raw", "file.gz" or die $!; open my $out, ">:raw", "output" or die $!; anyinflate($in => $out) or die "Decompression failed: $!"; # Use the OO interface use IO::Uncompress::AnyInflate; my $z = IO::Uncompress::AnyInflate->new("file.gz") or die "Could not open file.gz: $!"; my $content = $z->read(); $z->close(); 'DESCRIPTION': | This module provides a unified interface to decompress various compressed file formats, including those based on the zlib compression library (RFC 1950), DEFLATE (RFC 1951), gzip (RFC 1952), and zip. RFC 1950, RFC 1951 (optionally), gzip (RFC 1952), zip 'Functional Interface': | anyinflate $input_filename_or_reference => $output_filename_or_reference [, OPTS] A filename, A filehandle, A scalar reference, An array reference, An Input FileGlob string, A filename, A filehandle, A scalar reference, An Array Reference, An Output FileGlob Notes The input can be a filename, a filehandle, or a scalar reference containing the compressed data. The output can be a filename, a filehandle, or a scalar reference where the decompressed data will be stored. If the input is a filename and the output is a filename, the decompression will be performed directly from the input file to the output file. If the input is a filehandle and the output is a filehandle, the decompression will be performed from the input filehandle to the output filehandle. If the input is a scalar reference and the output is a scalar reference, the decompression will be performed from the scalar reference to the scalar reference. If the input is a filename and the output is a scalar reference, the decompression will be performed from the input file to the scalar reference. If the input is a scalar reference and the output is a filename, the decompression will be performed from the scalar reference to the output file. Optional Parameters "AutoClose => 0|1" If set to 1, the input and output filehandles will be closed after decompression. Default is 0. "BinModeOut => 0|1" If set to 1, the output filehandle will be opened in binary mode. Default is 0. "Append => 0|1" If set to 1, the decompressed data will be appended to the output file. Default is 0. A Buffer The input can be a Buffer object. A Filename The input can be a filename. A Filehandle The input can be a filehandle. "MultiStream => 0|1" If set to 1, the input may contain multiple compressed streams. Default is 0. "TrailingData => $scalar" If set, any trailing data after the compressed stream will be stored in this scalar. OneShot Examples # Decompress a gzip file to a scalar my $uncompressed = anyinflate("file.gz") or die "Decompression failed: $!"; # Decompress a zip file to a file anyinflate("archive.zip" => "output.tar") or die "Decompression failed: $!"; # Decompress a gzip stream to a filehandle open my $in, "<:raw", "file.gz" or die $!; open my $out, ">:raw", "output" or die $!; anyinflate($in => $out) or die "Decompression failed: $!"; 'OO Interface': | Constructor A filename, A filehandle, A scalar reference The constructor takes the same arguments as the functional interface. Constructor Options "AutoClose => 0|1" If set to 1, the input and output filehandles will be closed after decompression. Default is 0. "MultiStream => 0|1" If set to 1, the input may contain multiple compressed streams. Default is 0. "Prime => $string" If set, this string will be prepended to the decompressed data. "Transparent => 0|1" If set to 1, the module will attempt to transparently handle compressed and uncompressed data. Default is 0. "BlockSize => $num" The block size for reading and writing data. Default is 4096. InputLength => $size The expected size of the input data. This can be used to optimize memory allocation. "Append => 0|1" If set to 1, the decompressed data will be appended to the output file. Default is 0. "Strict => 0|1" If set to 1, the module will strictly enforce the format of the compressed data. Default is 0. "RawInflate => 0|1" If set to 1, the module will perform raw DEFLATE decompression without any framing (e.g., gzip or zlib headers). Default is 0. "ParseExtra => 0|1" If the gzip FEXTRA header field is present and this option is set, it will force the module to check that it conforms to the sub-field structure as defined in RFC 1952 'Methods': | read read getline getc ungetc inflateSync getHeaderInfo tell eof seek binmode opened autoflush input_line_number fileno close nextStream >

JSON::PP - interface to a pure Perl JSON encoder/decoder

SYNOPSIS
use JSON::PP;

my $scalar = decode_json('{"foo": 1}');
my $ref = decode_json('[1, "two", 3]');
my $json = encode_json([1, "two", 3]);
print $json; # [1,"two",3]
DESCRIPTION
The JSON::PP module provides an interface to a JSON encoder and decoder written in pure Perl. It is intended as a fallback for environments where a C compiler is not available, or where a pure Perl solution is preferred.
NOTE ON JSON::XS
If JSON::XS is installed, it will be used automatically by this module. If you want to force the use of the pure Perl implementation, you can set the $JSON::PP::PERL_ONLY variable to true.
OPTIONS
The encoder and decoder methods can be configured with a number of options. These can be passed as key-value pairs to the encode_json and decode_json functions, or set globally in the JSON::PP package.
GLOBAL SETTINGS
The following options can be set globally, and will affect all subsequent calls to encode_json and decode_json unless overridden:
use_utf8
Enable/disable UTF-8 support. Defaults to enabled.
allow_singlequote
Allow single quotes in strings. Defaults to false.
allow_barekey
Allow bare keys (unquoted strings) in objects. Defaults to false.
allow_nonref
Allow non-reference values in arrays and objects. Defaults to false.
allow_unknown
Allow unknown/unsupported data types. Defaults to false.
allow_blessed
Allow blessed objects in Perl data structures. Defaults to false.
convert_blessed
Convert blessed objects with a TO_JSON method. Defaults to false.
allow_tags
Allow tagged values (e.g., "(TAG)value"). Defaults to false.
indent_length
Number of spaces to use for indentation. Defaults to 2.
sort_by
A code reference to sort object keys by. Defaults to undef (no sorting).
max_depth
Maximum nesting depth for JSON structures. Defaults to 100.
max_size
Maximum size (in bytes) for JSON input. Defaults to 1MB.
FUNCTIONS
The following functions are exported by default:
encode_json( DATA, OPT => VAL, ... )
Encodes a Perl data structure into a JSON string. Options can be passed as key-value pairs.
decode_json( JSON, OPT => VAL, ... )
Decodes a JSON string into a Perl data structure. Options can be passed as key-value pairs.
is_json( STRING )
Returns true if the given string is valid JSON, false otherwise.
JSON::PP::Boolean
A dummy class to represent JSON boolean values. Use JSON::PP->true and JSON::PP->false to create instances.
JSON::PP::null
A singleton object to represent JSON null values.
SPECIAL VALUES
The module also provides constants for true, false and null:
JSON::PP->true
JSON::PP->false
JSON::PP->null
EXAMPLES
use JSON::PP;

my $data = {
    name    => "John Doe",
    age     => 30,
    is_active => JSON::PP->true,
    tags    => ["perl", "json"],
    address => undef,
};

my $json_string = encode_json($data, indent_length => 4, sort_by => sub { $_[0] cmp $_[1] });
print $json_string;

my $decoded_data = decode_json($json_string);
ENCODING
The following Perl data types are encoded as follows:
Perl Hash References
JSON Objects
Perl Array References
JSON Arrays
Scalars (Strings, Numbers, Booleans)
JSON Strings, Numbers, Booleans
Undefined Values
JSON null
Blessed Objects
Depends on options (allow_blessed, convert_blessed, allow_tags). See the OBJECT SERIALISATION section.
DECODING
The following JSON data types are decoded as follows:
JSON Objects
Perl Hash References
JSON Arrays
Perl Array References
JSON Strings
Perl Scalars (potentially with "use_utf8" flag set)
JSON Numbers
Perl Numbers
JSON Booleans
JSON::PP->true or JSON::PP->false
JSON Null
Perl undef
Comments
Shell-style comments (starting with #) are supported and ignored.
Tagged Values
Tagged values (e.g., "(TAG)value") are parsed if allow_tags is enabled. The tag and value are returned as a two-element array reference.
FLAGS (JSON::PP only)
These flags only apply when using the pure Perl implementation.
allow_singlequote
Allow single quotes in strings.
allow_barekey
Allow bare keys (unquoted strings) in objects.
allow_bignum
Allow parsing of large numbers as Perl's Math::BigInt/BigFloat objects. Requires these modules to be installed.
loose
Enable several less strict parsing options (equivalent to allow_singlequote, allow_barekey, allow_comments).
escape_slash
Escape forward slashes in strings (\/). Defaults to false.
indent_length
Number of spaces to use for indentation when encoding. Defaults to 2.
sort_by
A code reference that takes two keys and returns true if the first key should come before the second. Used for sorting object keys during encoding. Defaults to undef (no sorting).
allow_unknown
Allow encoding of unknown/unsupported data types. Defaults to false. Unknown types will be encoded as null.
allow_nonref
Allow non-reference values in arrays and objects. Defaults to false. When enabled, scalars will be encoded directly.
allow_blessed
Allow encoding of blessed objects. Defaults to false. When enabled, blessed objects will be encoded as their stringified representation (e.g., "SomeClass=HASH(0x...)").
convert_blessed
Convert blessed objects that have a TO_JSON method. Defaults to false.
allow_tags
Allow encoding of tagged values. Defaults to false. When enabled, objects with a FREEZE method will be encoded as "(TAG)value".
max_depth
Maximum nesting depth for JSON structures. Defaults to 100.
max_size
Maximum size (in bytes) for JSON input. Defaults to 1MB.
canonical
Produce canonical JSON output (sorted keys, no unnecessary whitespace). Overrides indent_length and sort_by.
boolean_values
A string specifying how to represent boolean values. Can be "true", "false", or "perl". Defaults to "perl" (uses JSON::PP->true and JSON::PP->false).
core_bools
Use Perl's core boolean values (1 and 0) instead of JSON::PP->true and JSON::PP->false. Defaults to false.
filter_json_object
A code reference used to filter keys from JSON objects during decoding. It receives the key and value, and should return true to keep the key-value pair.
filter_json_single_key_object
A code reference used to filter single-key JSON objects during decoding. It receives the key and value, and should return true to keep the object.
shrink
Remove all whitespace from the output JSON string. Equivalent to indent_length => 0.
encode
Encode Perl data to JSON.
decode
Decode JSON string to Perl data.
decode_prefix
Decode JSON string that may be prefixed with non-JSON data. The prefix is discarded.
FLAGS FOR JSON::PP ONLY
These flags are specific to the pure Perl implementation.
allow_singlequote
Allow single quotes in strings.
allow_barekey
Allow bare keys (unquoted strings) in objects.
allow_bignum
Allow parsing of large numbers as Perl's Math::BigInt/BigFloat objects.
loose
Enable several less strict parsing options.
escape_slash
Escape forward slashes in strings (\/).
indent_length
Number of spaces to use for indentation when encoding. Defaults to 2.
sort_by
A code reference that takes two keys and returns true if the first key should come before the second. Used for sorting object keys during encoding.
INCREMENTAL PARSING
The following options can be used for incremental parsing:
incr_parse
Enable incremental parsing mode.
incr_text
The text to be parsed incrementally.
incr_skip
Number of characters to skip from the beginning of the text.
incr_reset
Reset the incremental parser state.
MAPPING
The following mappings are used:
JSON -> PERL
object, array, string, number, true, false, null, shell-style comments ("# text"), tagged values ("(tag)value")
PERL -> JSON
hash references, array references, other references, JSON::PP::true, JSON::PP::false, JSON::PP::null, blessed objects, simple scalars
OBJECT SERIALISATION
1. "allow_tags" is enabled and the object has a "FREEZE" method, 2. "convert_blessed" is enabled and the object has a "TO_JSON" method, 3. "allow_bignum" is enabled and the object is a "Math::BigInt" or "Math::BigFloat", 4. "allow_blessed" is enabled, 5. none of the above
ENCODING/CODESET FLAG NOTES
"utf8" flag disabled, "utf8" flag enabled, "latin1" or "ascii" flags enabled
BUGS
Please report bugs to <bug-json-pp@rt.cpan.org>.

List::Util - A selection of general-utility list subroutines

SYNOPSIS
use List::Util qw(sum max min reduce);

my @numbers = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5);
print sum(@numbers), "\n";       # 15
print max(@numbers), "\n";       # 5
print min(@numbers), "\n";       # 1
print reduce { $a + $b } 0, @numbers, "\n"; # 15
DESCRIPTION
This module provides a selection of general-utility subroutines for manipulating lists. Many of these operations are common in functional programming languages and can be useful for simplifying Perl code.
LIST-REDUCTION FUNCTIONS
These functions reduce a list to a single value.
reduce
Takes a binary function, an initial value, and a list, and applies the function cumulatively to the items of the list, from left to right, so as to reduce the list to a single value. For example, reduce { $a + $b } 0, @list will sum the elements of @list.
reductions
Similar to reduce, but returns a list of all intermediate results, including the initial value.
any
Takes a predicate function and a list. Returns true if the predicate returns true for any element of the list.
all
Takes a predicate function and a list. Returns true if the predicate returns true for all elements of the list.
none
Takes a predicate function and a list. Returns true if the predicate returns false for all elements of the list.
notall
Takes a predicate function and a list. Returns true if the predicate returns false for at least one element of the list.
first
Takes a predicate function and a list. Returns the first element of the list for which the predicate returns true. Returns undef if no such element is found.
max
Returns the maximum value in the list. Uses the standard Perl comparison operators.
maxstr
Returns the maximum value in the list, using string comparison.
min
Returns the minimum value in the list. Uses the standard Perl comparison operators.
minstr
Returns the minimum value in the list, using string comparison.
product
Returns the product of all elements in the list.
sum
Returns the sum of all elements in the list.
sum0
Same as sum, but returns 0 for an empty list instead of undef.
KEY/VALUE PAIR LIST FUNCTIONS
These functions operate on lists of key/value pairs, typically generated by a hash.
pairs
Takes a hash or a list of key/value pairs and returns a flat list of alternating keys and values. This is useful for passing hash arguments to subroutines that accept them.
unpairs
Takes a flat list of alternating keys and values and returns a hash reference.
pairkeys
Takes a hash or a list of key/value pairs and returns a list of the keys.
pairvalues
Takes a hash or a list of key/value pairs and returns a list of the values.
pairgrep
Takes a predicate function and a list of key/value pairs. Returns a new list of key/value pairs for which the predicate returns true when applied to the key and value.
pairfirst
Takes a predicate function and a list of key/value pairs. Returns the first key/value pair for which the predicate returns true.
pairmap
Takes a code reference and a list of key/value pairs. Applies the code reference to each key/value pair and returns a new list of key/value pairs. The code reference should return a key/value pair.
OTHER FUNCTIONS
shuffle
Takes a list and returns a new list with the elements randomly shuffled. Uses the Fisher-Yates algorithm.
sample
Takes a number n and a list, and returns a new list containing n randomly selected elements from the original list, without replacement.
uniq
Returns a list with duplicate elements removed. The order of the remaining elements is preserved.
uniqint
Similar to uniq, but optimized for lists of integers.
uniqnum
Similar to uniq, but optimized for lists of numbers.
uniqstr
Similar to uniq, but optimized for lists of strings.
head
Takes a list and returns the first element. Equivalent to $list[0].
tail
Takes a list and returns a new list containing all elements except the first.
zip
Takes two or more lists and returns a new list of lists, where the i-th list contains the i-th element from each of the input lists.
mesh
Takes two or more lists and returns a list of all possible pairings of elements from the input lists. This is the Cartesian product of the lists.
CONFIGURATION VARIABLES
$RAND
A code reference that returns a random number between 0 and 1. Used by shuffle and sample. Can be replaced with a custom random number generator.
KNOWN BUGS
RT #95409
uniqnum() on oversized bignums can return incorrect results.
uniqnum() on oversized bignums
SUGGESTED ADDITIONS
A rotate function, a unique function that returns unique elements in the order they appear.

List::MoreUtils

List::Util::XS - Indicate if List::Util was compiled with a C compiler

SYNOPSIS
use List::Util::XS;

if (List::Util::XS::has_xs) {
    print "List::Util was compiled with a C compiler.\n";
} else {
    print "List::Util was compiled without a C compiler.\n";
}
DESCRIPTION
This module provides a single function, has_xs, which returns true if the List::Util module was compiled with a C compiler (i.e., if the XS version is available), and false otherwise.

Locale::Maketext - framework for localization

SYNOPSIS
use Locale::Maketext;

my $lh = Locale::Maketext->new;
# or
my $lh = Locale::Maketext->new( language => 'de' );

print $lh->maketext(
    "Hello, [_1]! You have [_2] new messages.",
    "World",
    10
);
# Output: Hallo, Welt! Sie haben 10 neue Nachrichten.
DESCRIPTION
This module provides a framework for internationalization and localization (i18n/l10n) of Perl applications. It allows you to manage translation files and retrieve translated strings based on the user's language preference.
QUICK OVERVIEW
The basic idea is to create a language-specific backend class that inherits from Locale::Maketext. This backend class defines a hash of messages and methods to retrieve them. The main Locale::Maketext object then uses this backend to fetch the appropriate translations.

Locale::Maketext::Lexicon - Base class for Locale::Maketext lexicons

SYNOPSIS

use Locale::Maketext::Lexicon;
# ...

DESCRIPTION

Locale::Maketext::Lexicon is the base class for all lexicons used by Locale::Maketext. It doesn't do much on its own, but it defines the methods that Locale::Maketext expects all its lexicons to implement.

You usually don't subclass this directly, but rather use one of its subclasses, like Locale::Maketext::Lexicon::Util or Locale::Maketext::Lexicon::Storable.

Subclassing Locale::Maketext::Lexicon

To subclass Locale::Maketext::Lexicon, you need to implement the following methods:

fetch
get_language

Utility Methods for Subclasses

The following methods are available for subclasses to use:

blacklist
$lh->blacklist(@list), $lh->allowlist(@list) or $lh->whitelist(@list)

Pod::Checker - comprueba documentos pod en busca de errores de sintaxis

SINOPSIS
OPCIONES/ARGUMENTOS
podchecker()
-warnings => val, -quiet => val
DESCRIPCIÓN
DIAGNÓSTICOS
Errores
empty =headn, =over en la línea N sin =back, Olvidaste un '=back' antes de '=headN', ¿=over es lo último en el documento?, '=item' fuera de cualquier '=over', =back sin =over, No puede haber un 0 en =over N, =over debería ser: '=over' o '=over número_positivo', =begin TARGET sin un =end TARGET correspondiente, =begin sin un objetivo?, =end TARGET sin un =begin correspondiente, ¿'=end' sin un objetivo?, '=end TARGET' no es válido, =end CONTENT no coincide con =begin TARGET, ¿=for sin objetivo?, enlace interno no resuelto NAME, Directiva desconocida: CMD, Eliminando código de formato desconocido SEQ, Secuencia SEQ<> no terminada, E<...> rodeando contenido extraño, E<> vacío, X<> vacío, Texto espurio después de =pod / =cut, =back no acepta parámetros, pero dijiste =back ARGUMENTO, ¡Las directivas =pod no deberían tener más de una línea! Ignorando N líneas de contenido, =cut encontrado fuera de un bloque pod, Sintaxis de =encoding inválida: CONTENT
Advertencias
comandos anidados CMD<...CMD<...>...>, múltiples ocurrencias (N) del objetivo de enlace name, línea que solo contiene espacios en blanco en un párrafo, =item no tiene contenido, No puedes tener =items (como en la línea N) a menos que lo primero después del =over sea un =item, Se esperaba '=item VALOR ESPERADO', Se esperaba '=item *', Posible desajuste de tipo de =item: se encontró 'x' liderando una supuesta definición =item, Tienes '=item x' en lugar del esperado '=item N', Contenido E desconocido en E<CONTENIDO>, bloque =over/=back vacío, sección vacía en párrafo anterior, Párrafo literal en sección NAME, =headn sin nivel superior precedente, Un Z<> no vacío
Hipervínculos
ignorando espacios en blanco al principio/final en el enlace, el texto/nodo alternativo '%s' contiene | o / sin escapar
VALOR DE RETORNO
EJEMPLOS

Pod::Perldoc - a front-end to Pod::Perldoc

SYNOPSIS
DESCRIPTION
This module is a front-end to the Pod::Perldoc module. It is designed to provide a convenient way to view POD documentation from within Perl programs, or to otherwise process POD data.

It has a number of backends that can format POD in various ways: Pod::Perldoc::ToTerm for terminal output, Pod::Perldoc::ToHtml for HTML output, Pod::Perldoc::ToRtf for RTF output, Pod::Perldoc::ToXml for XML output, Pod::Perldoc::ToText for plain text output, and Pod::Perldoc::ToNroff for nroff output. It also has Pod::Perldoc::ToPod which does no formatting at all, and Pod::Perldoc::ToTk which uses Tk::Pod to render POD.

The main program, perldoc , uses this module. You can too:

  use Pod::Perldoc;
  my $p = Pod::Perldoc->new;
  $p->run;

Or you can use one of the backends directly:

  use Pod::Perldoc::ToTerm;
  my $formatter = Pod::Perldoc::ToTerm->new;
  $formatter->parse_file(
      "/path/to/some/module.pm"
  );
CAVEAT
This module is a part of the Perl documentation system, and is not intended for use by end-users. If you are trying to view POD documentation, please use the perldoc command.

Also, the Tk backend is not part of the core Pod::Perldoc distribution. You will need to install Tk::Pod separately.

SEE ALSO

Pod::Perldoc::ToTerm - render Pod with terminal escapes

SYNOPSIS
DESCRIPTION
This module is a backend for Pod::Perldoc that formats POD data for display on a terminal. It supports basic formatting such as bold, italics, and code, as well as lists and tables.

It is not intended for direct use by end-users. If you want to view POD documentation on your terminal, please use the perldoc command.

PAGER FORMATTING
This formatter will attempt to detect if the output is going to a terminal, and if so, will use ANSI escape sequences to render bold and italics. It will also attempt to detect if the output is going to a pager (like `more` or `less`), and if so, will disable color output.

You can override this behavior by setting the $Pod::Perldoc::ToTerm::NoColor variable to a true value. This will disable all color output.

CAVEAT
This module is not intended for use by end-users. It is a backend for Pod::Perldoc , and is only useful when called by that module.

Pod::Simple - framework for parsing Pod

SYNOPSIS
DESCRIPTION
This is the base class for all Pod::Simple formatters. It provides a framework for parsing Pod documents and converting them into various formats.

The primary interface to Pod::Simple is through its subclasses. For example, to convert a Pod document to plain text, you would use Pod::Simple::Text :

  use Pod::Simple::Text;
  my $parser = Pod::Simple::Text->new;
  $parser->parse_file( "SomeModule.pm" );

You can also use the filter class method to do this more concisely:

  use Pod::Simple::Text;
  Pod::Simple::Text->filter( "SomeModule.pm" );

This module provides the core parsing engine and a common set of methods for all Pod::Simple formatters.

MAIN METHODS
"$parser = SomeClass->new();", "$parser->output_fh( *OUT );", "$parser->output_string( \$somestring );", "$parser->parse_file( $some_filename );", "$parser->parse_file( *INPUT_FH );", "$parser->parse_string_document( $all_content );", "$parser->parse_lines( ...@lines..., undef );", "$parser->content_seen", "SomeClass->filter( $filename );", "SomeClass->filter( *INPUT_FH );", "SomeClass->filter( \$document_content );"
SECONDARY METHODS
"$parser->parse_characters( SOMEVALUE )", "$parser->no_whining( SOMEVALUE )", "$parser->no_errata_section( SOMEVALUE )", "$parser->complain_stderr( SOMEVALUE )", "$parser->source_filename", "$parser->doc_has_started", "$parser->source_dead", "$parser->strip_verbatim_indent( SOMEVALUE )", "$parser->expand_verbatim_tabs( n )"
TERTIARY METHODS
"$parser->abandon_output_fh()", "$parser->abandon_output_string()", "$parser->accept_code( @codes )", "$parser->accept_codes( @codes )", "$parser->accept_directive_as_data( @directives )", "$parser->accept_directive_as_processed( @directives )", "$parser->accept_directive_as_verbatim( @directives )", "$parser->accept_target( @targets )", "$parser->accept_target_as_text( @targets )", "$parser->accept_targets( @targets )", "$parser->accept_targets_as_text( @targets )", "$parser->any_errata_seen()", "$parser->errata_seen()", "$parser->detected_encoding()", "$parser->encoding()", "$parser->parse_from_file( $source, $to )", "$parser->scream( @error_messages )", "$parser->unaccept_code( @codes )", "$parser->unaccept_codes( @codes )", "$parser->unaccept_directive( @directives )", "$parser->unaccept_directives( @directives )", "$parser->unaccept_target( @targets )", "$parser->unaccept_targets( @targets )", "$parser->version_report()", "$parser->whine( @error_messages )"
ENCODING
Pod::Simple attempts to detect the encoding of the Pod document. If it can't, it defaults to "UTF-8". You can override this by passing an encoding parameter to the new or filter methods: 
  my $parser = Pod::Simple::Text->new( encoding => 'iso-8859-1' );
  Pod::Simple::Text->filter( $file, encoding => 'iso-8859-1' );

Pod::Simple::Convert -- parse and process POD documentation

This module provides the main interface for parsing POD documents and turning them into other formats.

There are many modules that provide different output formats for POD. They are all subclass of this one.

SYNOPSIS
    use Pod::Simple::Convert;
    my $ps = Pod::Simple::Convert->new;
    $ps->convert_trees(\*STDIN, \*STDOUT);
DESCRIPTION

The primary purpose of this class is to provide a common interface to all the Pod::Simple output handlers.

The main method here is convert_trees.

METHODS
new
new()
Creates a new Pod::Simple::Convert object.
convert_trees
convert_trees( $input_stream, $output_stream )
This method takes POD input from $input_stream (which can be a filehandle, a filename, or an arrayref of filenames) and processes it, writing the output to $output_stream (which can be a filehandle or a filename).
convert_trees
convert_trees( $input_stream, $output_stream, $output_handler_class )
This method is similar to the above, but also takes an optional third argument: $output_handler_class.
If this argument is provided, the method will use that class to process the POD. This is the preferred way to use this method.
convert_trees
convert_trees( $input_stream, $output_stream, $output_handler_object )
This method is similar to the above, but also takes an optional third argument: $output_handler_object.
If this argument is provided, the method will use that object to process the POD.

TAP::Parser::Scheduler - Programa pruebas durante la ejecución paralela

VERSION
SINOPSIS
DESCRIPCIÓN
MÉTODOS
Métodos de clase
Estructura de datos de reglas
Por defecto, todas las pruebas son elegibles para ejecutarse en paralelo. La especificación de cualquiera de sus propias reglas elimina esta, "Gana la primera coincidencia". La primera regla que coincida con una prueba será la que se aplique. Cualquier prueba que no coincida con una regla se ejecutará en secuencia al final de la ejecución. La existencia de una regla no implica la selección de una prueba. Todavía debe especificar las pruebas a ejecutar. La especificación de una regla para permitir que las pruebas se ejecuten en paralelo no hace que la ejecución sea paralela. Todavía necesita especificar el número de "jobs" paralelos en su objeto Harness.

Test2::Manual::Anatomy::EndToEnd - Visión general de Test2 desde la carga hasta el final.

DESCRIPCIÓN
¿QUÉ SUCEDE CUANDO CARGO LA API?
Se crea una instancia singleton de Test2::API::Instance, Se definen varias funciones de API que utilizan la instancia singleton, ¿Luego qué?
¿QUÉ SUCEDE CUANDO USO UNA HERRAMIENTA?
Se ejecuta una función de herramienta, La herramienta adquiere un objeto de contexto, La herramienta utiliza el objeto de contexto para crear, enviar y devolver eventos, Cuando termina, la herramienta DEBE liberar el contexto, La herramienta devuelve
¿QUÉ SUCEDE CUANDO ADQUIERO UN CONTEXTO?
$!, $@, $? y $^E se capturan y preservan, El estado de la API se cambia a 'cargado', Se encuentra el hub actual, Se activan los hooks de adquisición de contexto, Se encuentra cualquier contexto existente, Se mide la profundidad de la pila, Se crea un nuevo contexto (si no se encontró un contexto existente), Se activan los hooks de inicialización de contexto (si no se encontró un contexto existente), Se restauran $!, $@, $? y $^E, Se devuelve el contexto
¿QUÉ SUCEDE CUANDO ENVÍO UN EVENTO?
Se carga el módulo Test2::Event::Ok, Se crea una nueva instancia de Test2::Event::Ok, El objeto de evento se envía al hub, El hub ejecuta el evento a través de cualquier filtro, El estado global de la prueba se actualiza para reflejar el evento, El evento se envía al formateador, El evento se envía a todos los listeners
¿QUÉ SUCEDE CUANDO LIBERO UN CONTEXTO?
Se libera el clon del contexto actual, Si este era el contexto canónico, realmente se liberará, Se llaman los hooks de liberación, El contexto se borra, Se restauran $!, $@, $? y $^E
¿QUÉ SUCEDE CUANDO USO done_testing()?
Se recopilarán los eventos IPC pendientes, Se ejecutarán los hooks de seguimiento, Se generará y procesará el evento de plan final, Se finalizará el hub actual
¿QUÉ SUCEDE CUANDO UN SCRIPT DE PRUEBA TERMINA?
Se comprueban las versiones de la API, Cualquier resto

Test2 - A Fast, Feature Rich, and Extensible Test Framework

This is a test framework designed for speed and extensibility. It is built upon the ideas of Test::More, but aims to be faster, more feature-rich, and easier to extend.

DESCRIPTION

The Test2 framework is a set of modules designed to make testing in Perl faster, more robust, and more flexible. It is built with an emphasis on performance and extensibility, allowing developers to create custom testing tools and integrate them seamlessly.

Key features include:

  • Speed: Optimized for fast execution, especially in large test suites.

  • Extensibility: Designed to be easily extended with new tools, plugins, and bundles.

  • Rich Feature Set: Provides a comprehensive set of features for common testing needs.

  • Compatibility: Aims for compatibility with existing testing practices and tools where possible.

EXPLANATION
Test2 is a next-generation testing framework for Perl. It aims to improve upon existing frameworks like Test::More by offering better performance, more features, and a more flexible architecture. The framework is composed of several core components and a rich ecosystem of extensions. It's designed to be the foundation for all testing needs, from simple unit tests to complex integration and release testing.
SEE ALSO
Test2::Require::RealFork, Test2::Require::Threads
SOURCE
MAINTAINERS
Chad Granum <exodist@cpan.org>
AUTHORS
Chad Granum <exodist@cpan.org>

Test2::Require::Module - Skip tests if certain packages are not installed, or insufficient versions.

DESCRIPTION
This module provides a simple way to skip tests if specific Perl modules are not installed or if their installed versions do not meet a required minimum.
SYNOPSIS
use Test2::Require::Module qw(Some::Module Some::Other::Module);
# OR
use Test2::Require::Module 'Some::Module:v1.2.3';

done_testing;

This module checks if the underlying operating system supports true fork() behavior. If not, tests using this module will be skipped. This is important for tests that rely on process forking.

Test2::Require::Threads - Skip a test file unless the system supports threading

DESCRIPTION
This module checks if the underlying operating system and Perl installation support threading. If threading is not supported, tests using this module will be skipped.
SYNOPSIS
use Test2::Require::Threads;

# Tests below this line require threading support
EXPLANATION
This module is essential for testing code that uses Perl threads. It ensures that such tests are only executed on platforms where threading is actually functional, preventing unexpected failures due to lack of support.

Test2::Suite - Distribution with a rich set of tools built upon the Test2 framework.

DESCRIPTION

Test2::Suite is a meta-distribution that bundles together a comprehensive set of tools, plugins, and requirement checkers for the Test2 testing framework. It aims to provide a batteries-included experience for Perl testing.

WHAT ARE TOOLS, PLUGINS, AND BUNDLES?
Tools
Provide specific testing functionalities, such as assertions, comparisons, and subtest execution.
Plugins
Modify the behavior of the Test2 framework, like controlling test exit codes or reporting.
Bundles
Collections of tools and plugins designed for specific testing scenarios or preferences.
INCLUDED BUNDLES
Test2::V#, Extended, More, Simple
INCLUDED TOOLS
Basic, Compare, ClassicCompare, Class, Defer, Encoding, Exports, Mock, Ref, Spec, Subtest, Target
INCLUDED PLUGINS
BailOnFail, DieOnFail, ExitSummary, SRand, UTF8
INCLUDED REQUIREMENT CHECKERS
AuthorTesting, EnvVar, Fork, RealFork, Module, Perl, Threads
SEE ALSO
CONTACTING US
For bug reports, feature requests, or general discussion, please visit the Test2 project repository or mailing list.

Test2::Todo - TODO extension for Test2.

DESCRIPTION
This module provides a mechanism to mark tests as TODO within the Test2 framework. It allows you to specify a reason for the TODO and optionally associate it with a specific test hub.
SYNOPSIS
use Test2::Todo reason => 'This feature is not yet implemented';

subtest 'This part needs implementation' => sub {
    # ... tests that are currently TODO ...
};

# Or associate with a specific hub
my $hub = Test2::Hub::new();
my $todo = Test2::Todo->new(reason => 'Known bug', hub => $hub);
CONSTRUCTION OPTIONS
reason (required), hub (optional)
INSTANCE METHODS
$todo->end
CLASS METHODS
$count = Test2::Todo->hub_in_todo($hub)
OTHER NOTES
When a Test2::Todo object is destroyed, it automatically calls its end method, which finalizes the TODO status for the associated tests.
How it works
Test2::Todo works by intercepting test results and marking them as TODO based on the provided reason. When the object goes out of scope or is explicitly ended, it ensures that the TODO status is correctly reported.
$todo->end is called at destruction
This is a key feature ensuring that TODO markers are properly managed even if explicit cleanup is forgotten.
Can I use multiple instances?
Yes, you can create multiple Test2::Todo instances, each with its own reason and optionally associated with different test hubs.

Test2::Tools - Documentation for Tools.

DESCRIPTION
This module serves as a central point for documentation related to Test2 tools. It explains the philosophy behind Test2 tools, how to write them, and answers frequently asked questions.
FAQ
Why is it called Test2::Tools, and not Test2::Tool?
The plural form is used because this module documents the concept of "tools" within the Test2 framework, which encompasses various utilities and helper modules.
Should my tools subclass Test2::Tools?
No, Test2::Tools itself is not meant to be subclassed. Instead, it provides guidance on how to structure your own tool modules.
HOW DO I WRITE A 'TOOLS' MODULE?
Writing a Test2::Tools module involves creating a Perl module that provides a set of related testing utilities. These tools are typically loaded and used within test files to perform assertions, comparisons, or other testing tasks. The documentation outlines best practices for naming, structure, and integration.
